Autonomy is not autocracy

In response to my appeal to the Chief Minister to “Give Sarawakian’s a Voice” by implementing local council elections in tandem with developments in the rest of Malaysia, PBB’s propaganda machine responded and says that it is wrong to criticise the Chief Minister for wanting local council elections and suggests that the CM’s views are infallible because Abang Jo, ‘banyak makan garam.’

It also suggests that Pakatan Harapan’s on going implementation of local council elections is hypocritical as Tun Mahathir has gone against it in the past.

However, this only proves that Pakatan Harapan is a democratic & dynamic coalition, made strong because different ideas are all taken into consideration. This show even though the Prime Minister may personally disagree with a policy, it is clear that if Cabinet as a whole approves of it, it will be put to a vote in Parliament. PH acts as a democracy, where conflicting opinions have their say in arriving at decisions.

It seems such a concept is foreign to GPS (formerly BN) , as after all they have never once disagreed with the Chief Minister. GPS, an incarnation of the Barisan Nasional repeats the mantra of ‘jangan lawan tauke’ where dissent is clamped down upon, where over the decades despite many anti-Sarawakian policies of the BN era, component parties of the local BN such as SUPP and PBB refused to oppose and even participated freely in the erosion of Sarawakian rights. Remember, that even when Datuk Seri Najib was embroiled in the 1MDB scandal, Abang Johari pledged total support for him in the federal election. Furthermore, Abang Jo is acting like a warlord presiding over his subjects asking local councillors and village chiefs to ‘go to war’ in upcoming elections. This is not giving back autonomy to Sarawakians, this is very much consolidation of the autocratic nature of his GPS government.

In contrast PH is a party which allows for autonomy to disagree and to influence decisions. The opinions of even the Prime Minister are secondary to the democratic will of the people. Such autonomy is something that local council elections would bring to Sarawak and which PH is intent on giving to Sarawakians.

Looking further at PH (or in a “mirror” as the reply suggests), and all I see is a new government that listens to its people, while when I look at GPS/ ex BN, I see the ones who presided over more than 50 years of erosion of Sarawakian rights, I see accomplices who are in a hurry to distanced themselves from acts which they were complicit , as if changing a name would cause a whole generation of Sarawakians to suffer collectively amnesia. PKR Sarawak is intent on getting back for the people what they have lost in the last 50+ years.

The people can judge for themselves such conduct which  was clearly reflected in the recent Parliamnetary Voting on the constitutional amendment to recognise Sarawak as equal partners. This was clearly the first step and would have set the footing to returning autonomy to Sarawak, the record shows that GPS/ex BN abstained which ended up scuttling the whole process.  They use doublespeak to suggest that PH are eating away at the state rights of Sarawak, but in truth, we lost most of those rights away long ago under their regime.

Even now they act as if they know more than everyone, condescendingly pointing out that Zohari “banyak makan garam” and suggesting that what he says is beyond contestation. Applying this warped logic, we cannot ever disagree with anyone who ‘banyak makan garam’, are they suggesting that the Rakyat are servants, who should hand over all our rights to them as masters? or are they are just plain ‘salty’ because their party does not allow them to think for themselves ? If so don’t spread your “jangan lawan tauke” culture to our future generations. Our youths deserve more respect as the future of our country,  further as Sarawakians all deserve to be listened to, they deserve autonomy not in the form of autocracy but democracy.

FORMATION OF MALAYSIA : FLASH BACK

December 1962, the Chief Secretary and leader of the Sarawak delegation to the Inter-Governmental Committee meetings, MR F.D Jakeway stated that Sarawak would have 24 seats in the Malaysia House of Representatives.

Tunku Abdul Rahman said that Malaysia would come into being on August 31, next year even though there might be an EMERGENCY in the Borneo Territories and he warned that he would “go all out to smash” any elements trying to create unrest and chaos when Malaysia was formed.

Chairman of the Sarawak Chinese Association Mr Ling Beng Siew said on his return from an Inter-Governmental Committee meeting in Kuala Lumpur that he wished to tell all Sarawak Chinese that they would be given citizenship and the qualifications for it would be very simple.

January 1963, the year will be an historic one for Sarawak to joined in a new independent Federation of Malaysia as an equal partner with Malaya, Sabah and with Singapore, said the Governor of Sarawak, Sir Alexander Waddell in a New Year message broadcast to the people.

The SUPP issued a statement saying that it had decided to send a fresh anti-Malaysia memorandum to the United Nations. Pasok Momugum withdrew from the memorandum when it decided to support Malaysia.

February 1963, The Sarawak Alliance launched itself into the International arena to clarify its stand on the Malaysia issues by :
 
Appealing to President Soekarno not to intervene in Sarawak’s progress towards independence through Malaysia.
Informing the Secretary-General of the United Nations, U Thant, that it wished to represent its case against the SUPP on the Malaysia issue.

February, 1963 The Sarawak Alliance disclosed the contents of a memorandum it had sent to the United Nations challenging the SUPP criticisms levelled against the Malaysia Plan and alleged that the policies of the SUPP were communist dominated.

The Sarawak Chinese Association released for publication its manifesto which expressed support for Malaysia. 

A group of 16 religious leaders from Sarawak and North Borneo who toured the Federation of Malaya said on their return that “a spirit of brotherhood and tolerance” pervaded life in Malaya.
February, 1963 Representatives of the pro-Malaysia political parties in the territories reaffirmed their strong support for federation at the conclusion of two-day conference held in Jesselton. 

The SUPP’s memorandum to United Nations was published. It contended that the country was made to join the proposed Federation of Malaysia in an “Undemocratic Manner.” The party also stated that it would agree to a United Nations enquiry to establish whether the claims and allegations made by the Sarawak Alliance’s memorandum to the United Nations were true.

February 1963, the Governor of Sarawak, Sir Alexander Waddell, in his Hari Raya message stressed that the people would have to bear heavier responsibilities when the country gained its independence in Malaysia. The Inter-Governmental Committee Report was published in Sarawak. Thousands of copies of the summarised version of the Report were distributed throughout the country in various languages. The Report contained generous terms and safeguards for Sarawak.

March 1963, Council Negeri took the vital decision to “sail in convoy with the Good Ship Malaysia” when it approved, without dissent, the Inter-Governmental Committee Report. All the Divisional Advisory Councils signified their acceptance of the Report as well.

Council Negeri also resolved, subject to the approval of Her Majesty Council, that Sarawak should have an almost fully elected legislature to Supreme Council headed by a Chief Minister before Malaysia Day. 

A petition of religious freedom in the proposed Federation of Malaysia signed by representatives of five Christian churches in Sarawak was presented to Council Negeri.

March 1963, The flag and anthem of the Rajahs were adopted as the State Flag and State Anthem of Sarawak

A two-day meeting of the Grand Alliance pro-Malaysia parties opened in Kuala Lumpur on March 30th. A delegation from the Sarawak Alliance attended it.

April 1963, Chief of the World Bank Malaysia Economic Mission and his team of experts paid a visit to Kuching in the course of their investigations into the economic implications of Malaysia. Later at July, his report stated that the proposed Federation of Malaysia would be a strong economic unit.

Party Negara Sarawak decided to withdraw from membership of the Sarawak Alliance. 

The United Nations Under-Secretary and Chief of Cabinet, Mr C.V Narasimhan, said at Kuching, no one had yet expressed opposition to the Malaysia concept - they were all striving to reach the same target but by different routes.

Election broadcast talks were made by six of the political parties contesting in Sarawak and five of the parties expressed full support for Malaysia.

May 1963, an Order-In-Council amending the Constitution of Sarawak so as to make Sarawak a new State within the Federation of Malaysia was signed by the Queen and published. The changes provided a fully democratic legislature to be set up before Malaysia Day.
3 Labour Members of  British Parliament visited Kuching in a fact finding mission and 2 of them recommended that the elections in Sarawak would be an indication of what people felt about Malaysia.

The report issued by Council Negri’s Public Petitions Committee after considering the petitions of the five Christian churches on religious freedom in Malaysia, said there was no reason to anticipate that after Malaysia was established there would be any interference in Sarawak with;
 “ Freedom to worship, practise, observe and teach and propagate, in accordance with the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights (Articles 18 and 19).”

June 1963, the Sarawak elections held during May and this month resulted in a victory for the pro-Malaysia political parties. The Sarawak Alliance capture 138 seats, Party Negara Sarawak with 59 seats, the independents 116 seats and the SUPP with 116 seats.

July 1963, in a surprise announcement, the anti-Malaysia SUPP party and the pro-Malaysia Party Negara Sarawak agreed to form a coalition in opposition to the Sarawak Alliance. 

July 9 1963, Representatives of Britain, Malaya, Singapore, North Borneo and Sarawak signed an agreement in London just after midnight July 9, creating the Federation of Malaysia. Sarawak signatories to the agreement were the Attorney-General, Mr. P.E.H Pike; Temenggong Jugah anak Barieng; the Datu Bandar, Abang Haji Mustapha; Mr Ling Beng Siew and Datu Abang Haji Openg.

July 15, 1963. The Divisional Advisory Council met to elect members to Council Negri. The elections resulted in triumph for the Alliance which had 23 of its members supporting councillors returned out of a total of 36.

This opened the way for the Sarawak Alliance to form the Government and it was announced on the 22 July 1963 that Mr Stephen Kalong Ningkan, the Alliance secretary-general, had been designated Chief Minister. Mr Kalong Ningkan was later appointed to be the first Chief Minister of Sarawak by the Governor of Sarawak, Sir Alexander Waddell, who also nominated three people to the Council Negri and established a new Supreme Council.

August 2, 1963, the ministries allocated to the members of the Supreme Council and approved by the Governor were officially announced. They were :
Mr Teo Kui Seng , Minister for Natural Resources, Encik Abdul Taib Bin Mahmud, Minister for Communications and Work, Mr Dunstan Endawi anak Enchana, Minister for Local Government, Awang Hipni bin Pengiran Annu and Mr James Wong Kim Ming, Minister of State.

It was also announced that Mr James Wong would be Deputy Chief Minister in charge of certain special duties. 

August 1963, At meeting held in Manila among the leaders of Malaya, the Philippines and Indonesia from July 30 to August 5, it was agreed that the United Nations Secretary-General, U Thant, or his representatives should ascertain, prior to the establishment of Malaysia, whether the people of Sabah and Sarawak wished to join the proposed Federation of Malaysia. 

The elected governments of Sarawak and Sabah Alliance Party mae it clear that they were determined to become independent states of Malaysia on August 31 but added that they were not opposed to the agreement reached at Manila that there should be a UN assessment.

August 1963 During the Manila conference, Chief Minister Mr Stephen Kalong Ningkan sent a telegram to U Thant stating that it was unnecessary to hold a referendum in Sarawak because the elections showed that the majority of the people supported Malaysia and that the Sarawak Alliance had already formed the Government.

August 16, 1963. A nine-man UN team led by Mr Laurence Michelmore, arrived in Kuching to ascertain the views of the Sabah and Sarawak people on Malaysia. The arrival was greeted by an anti-Malaysia demonstration staged mostly by young chinese. 

August 1963. The Sarawak Alliance issued a statement expressing regret at the decision to send the UN team to Sarawak and stated that it was confident that the findings would show once again that the majority of the people supported Malaysia.

August 1963, the Malayan Prime Minister said that he had given in to Indonesian demands at Manila for the sake of peace and for that reason, he had agreed to postpone thefoundation date of Malaysia past the scheduled August 31st.

Indonesia provoked another crisis over Malaysia by refusing to send the stipulated four observers to witness the UN assessment team at work in Sabah and Sarawak. At the same time it stepped up acts of border terrorism in an effort to create more confusion.  

These actions only serve to stiffen the determination of the people of Sarawak to achieve independence ( through Malaysia if possible) on August 31. 

August 1963, It was announced on Friday, August 23, that on August 31 a de facto self government in State affairs would exist in Sarawak whether or not there was a delay in the formation of Malaysia. 

The Sarawak Alliance in a cable to U Thant urged that the UN team should begin work as scheduled or be withdrawn. 

31 August 1963, The inauguration of the State Government was marked on August 31 by a midnight broadcast made by the Chief Minister, the sounding ships’ sirens and the playing of the State Anthem followed by a 21-gun salute from Fort Margherita in Kuching. 

The Chief Minister said in his broadcast;
 “Sarawak is entering a new era in its history. As an independent self-governing state it stands on the threshold of a promising future - a future that needs the full loyal co-operation of everyone of its loyal citizens.”

26 August 1963, The UN team began its tour of the country. The tour was marred by anti-Malaysia riots at Sibu, Miri and Bau. Hearinbgs ended on September 4.

Following talked in Kuala Lumpur and Singapore between leaders of the governments in the Malaysian territories and the Commonwealth and Colonial Secretary, Mr Duncan Sandys;

It was agreed that Malaysia should come into being on Monday, September 16.

對於檳城及雪蘭莪州的情況，黃慶偉解釋，行動黨与其盟友在這兩個州屬执政后，执意要实施地方议会选举，但遭首相纳吉和联邦政府诸多阻扰及反对。槟城州政府甚至因為此事而起诉联邦政府，直到联邦法院，为的就是要举行地方议会选举。

西马半岛州属之地方政府受到联邦法令管辖，也就是《1976年地方政府法令》，而砂拉越的26个地方政府卻不受这項联邦法令限制，因為我們擁有自己的法令，即《砂州1996年地方政府法令》。

“所以槟城及雪州要举行地方议会选举，就必须修改联邦的法令，但遭到纳吉和国阵国会议员大力反对，因为他们想把市长和市议员职位當成黨內資產，不是为了服务人民。”

DAP Padungan State Assemblyman YB Wong King Wei said that the Penang and Selangor government  cannot implement local government elections within their state due to its limitations within Federal Statutes on top of the opposition from the BN government.  However, Sarawak has autonomy in this matter and it does not require the Federal Government under Prime Minister Najib Razak to consent.

The Drainage and Irrigation Department (DID) has admitted that one of the reasons for occurrence of flash floods in the city is due to the clogged drainage systems.  Therefore, YB Wong King Wei suggested that Sarawak must restore the local council elections, to ensure the efficiency of the councils. However SUPP has issued a statement in response to Wong's suggestion, attacking DAP not implementing Local Government Election in Penang and Selangor, which is under the ruling of DAP and its alliance partners.

"I am extremely disappointed with SUPP. They portray themselves as a party who fights for the autonomy for the State, but they themselves actually do not know Sarawak have their own autonomy in local council matters, including local government election!"

"SUPP must do their homework to understand the rights of the people. Since they are even too lazy to do their homework, making accusations without proper backing, how can they fight for the benefits of the people? How can they fight for our autonomy?"

In the case of Penang and Selangor, YB Wong King Wei explained that DAP and its alliance partners have constantly insisted on the implementation of the local council elections, but  it was Prime Minister Najib Razak and the  Federal Government who stopped the process and caused so many other obstruction to it. The Penang State Government even went as far as suing the federal government, where the matter even went up until the Federal Court, in order for their rights to hold local council elections

In Peninsular Malaysia, the local government is subjected to Local Government Act 1976, which is Federal Law. 

However, Sarawak, which has a total of 26 local governments, is not subjected to the said Federal Statute, but our own Sarawak legislation, namely “Local Authorities Ordinance 1996”

Thus in Sarawak, it is different. We do not need to amend the Federal Act through parliament, but it only requires the State legislatures to amend the “Local Authorities Ordinance of Sarawak Act 1996,

Therefore, for Penang and Selangor to hold local council elections, the federal statute has to be amended in Parliament, which Najib and Barisan Nasional MPs have greatly opposed. This is because BN has always used the mayor and councillor positions within local council to serve their interest in consolidating their own power, and not to serve the interest of the people.

 
“It is obvious that DAP and its alliance partners have insisted in the implementation of local council elections in Penang and Selangor but they faced legal constraints as well as opposition from the BN government. It is a known fact but SUPP accusations towards DAP for not restoring local government elections clearly shows either their ignorance, or their own lack of understanding of the issue.

Furthermore, the Federal Constitution, where the provision in Article 95D and Article 95E clearly states that the Federal Government has no right to interfere in matters of local government of Sarawak and Sabah. This is where I have emphasized that we in Sarawak do have local council autonomy.

“Sarawak can hold its own local council elections without the consent of Najib as well as the agreement of the Federal Government. I am appalled at the lack of understanding by SUPP of the rights of Sarawak in the Constitution. No wonder the State led by SUPP who is part of the State government for decades, seem to be losing more and more of its rights.

ASEAN Stakeholder Engagement on Myanmar: Addressing the Five-Point Consensus, Upholding Democracy and Rejecting the Military’s Sham Elections 

Throughout Malaysia’s 2025 ASEAN Chairmanship, a series of Stakeholder Engagement Meetings on Myanmar (SEMs) were convened by the Special Envoy of the ASEAN Chair on Myanmar, bringing together key stakeholders - including representatives from the National Unity Government (NUG), the National Unity Consultative Council (NUCC), Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), Ethnic Resistance Organisations (EROs), Consultative Councils, Federal Units and various other representative bodies.  

These engagements have served as an inclusive platform to discuss the ongoing crisis in Myanmar, develop strategies and recommendations on the effective implementation of ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus including on cessation of violence, humanitarian assistance, and inclusive political dialogue, and to address the junta’s planned sham elections. 

Stakeholders at the SEMs reiterated grave concern over the deteriorating situation in Myanmar since the military coup of February 2021 and reaffirmed their shared commitment to restoring democracy and upholding human rights. While acknowledging ASEAN’s adoption of the Five-Point Consensus, stakeholders expressed alarm over its limited implementation amid the military’s continued violence against civilians and blatant disregard for democratic norms including the principles enshrined in the ASEAN Charter.

Key outcomes of the meeting included:
Rejection of the Military’s Sham Elections – Stakeholders unanimously condemned the junta’s planned elections as a façade designed to entrench military rule under the guise of democratic reform. These elections are also in direct defiance of ASEAN Five-Point Consensus, which prioritizes cessation of violence, inclusive political dialogue, and unhindered humanitarian assistance to all in need. Proceeding with unilateral elections amid ongoing violence, denial of aid, and exclusion of key stakeholders is illegitimate and a direct assault on ASEAN's mandate and credibility. Stakeholders stand united in rejecting the junta’s attempts to manipulate ASEAN to legitimize its own authority and road-map even while remaining in blatant non-compliance with the Five-Point Consensus.

Unity Among the Revolutionary Forces – The meeting underscored the importance of solidarity among all forces in advancing a shared vision for a federal democratic Myanmar.

Call for Decisive ASEAN Action – Stakeholders urged ASEAN to translate the Five-Point Consensus into tangible, time-bound measures that can meaningfully end violence, protect civilians, advance inclusive political dialogue and bring peace and stability to Myanmar. 

Humanitarian Imperative – Stakeholders called for immediate and sustained humanitarian support, emphasizing the importance of cross-border delivery mechanisms and partnerships with local and community-based organizations to ensure aid reaches those most in need - particularly in conflict zones. 

Inclusive Political Dialogue – The meetings reaffirmed that durable peace can only emerge from an inclusive political process involving all legitimate stakeholders - including the NUG, NUCC, EROs, and various representatives entities committed to six political objectives of federal democracy and system change. ASEAN’s engagement efforts must reflect this inclusivity to achieve sustainable peace through a meaningful and participatory approach. 

Regional Stability – Stakeholders highlighted that the military junta’s attempted coup and indiscriminate attacks on civilians have caused Myanmar’s crisis with deep regional implications, threatening cross-border security, migration stability, and economic integrity. A strong and unified ASEAN response is essential to prevent further deterioration of Southeast Asia’s collective peace and credibility.

In closing, stakeholders expressed deep appreciation to Malaysia for its leadership as ASEAN Chair and to the Special Envoy of the ASEAN Chair on Myanmar, HE Tan Sri Othman Hashim, for advancing an inclusive, principled approach to resolving the Myanmar crisis. 

The meeting concluded with a clear message: There is no path forward that legitimizes military rule. Any political or humanitarian framework must be rooted in the will and aspirations of the Myanmar people for peace, justice, democracy, and a federal union that guarantees equality for all.

The agreement
Point 1: Religion
While there was no objection to Islam being the national religion of Malaysia there should be no State religion in Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah), and the provisions relating to Islam in the present Constitution of Malaya should not apply to Borneo.

Point 2: Language
* a. Malay should be the national language of the Federation
* b. English should continue to be used for a period of 10 years after Malaysia Day
* c. English should be an official language of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) for all purposes, State or Federal, without limitation of time.

Point 3: Constitution
Whilst accepting that the present Constitution of the Federation of Malaya should form the basis of the Constitution of Malaysia, the Constitution of Malaysia should be a completely new document drafted and agreed in the light of a free association of states and should not be a series of amendments to a Constitution drafted and agreed by different states in totally different circumstances. A new Constitution for Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) was of course essential.

Point 4: Head of Federation
The Head of State in Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should not be eligible for election as Head of the Federation.

Point 5: Name of Federation
“Malaysia” but not “Melayu Raya”

Point 6: Immigration
Control over immigration into any part of Malaysia from outside should rest with the Central Government but entry into Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should also require the approval of the State Government. The Federal Government should not be able to veto the entry of persons into Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) for State Government purposes except on strictly security grounds. Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should have unfettered control over the movements of persons other than those in Federal Government employ from other parts of Malaysia Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah).

Point 7: Right of Secession
There should be no right to secede from the Federation

Point 8: Borneanisation
Borneanisation of the public service should proceed as quickly as possible.

Point 9: British Officers
Every effort should be made to encourage British Officers to remain in the public service until their places can be taken by suitably qualified people from Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah)

Point 10: Citizenship
The recommendation in paragraph 148(k) of the Report of the Cobbold Commission should govern the citizenship rights in the Federation of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) subject to the following amendments:
* a) sub-paragraph (i) should not contain the proviso as to five years residence
* b) in order to tie up with our law, sub-paragraph (ii)(a) should read “7 out of 10 years” instead of “8 out of 10 years”
* c) sub-paragraph (iii) should not contain any restriction tied to the citizenship of parents – a person born in Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) after Malaysia must be federal citizen.

Point 11: Tariffs and Finance
Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should retain control of its own finance, development and tariff, and should have the right to work up its own taxation and to raise loans on its own credit.

Point 12: Special position of indigenous races
In principle, the indigenous races of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should enjoy special rights analogous to those enjoyed by Malays in Malaya, but the present Malays’ formula in this regard is not necessarily applicable in Borneo(Sarawak & Sabah).

Point 13: State Government
* a) the Prime Minister should be elected by unofficial members of Legislative Council
* b) There should be a proper Ministerial system in Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah).

Point 14: Transitional period
This should be seven years and during such period legislative power must be left with the State of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) by the Constitution and not be merely delegated to the State Government by the Federal Government.

Point 15: Education
The existing educational system of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should be maintained and for this reason it should be under state control.

Point 16: Constitutional safeguards
No amendment modification or withdrawal of any special safeguard granted to Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should be made by the Central Government without the positive concurrence of the Government of the State of North Borneo

The power of amending the Constitution of the State of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should belong exclusively to the people in the state. (Note: The United Party, The Democratic Party and the Pasok Momogun Party considered that a three-fourth majority would be required in order to effect any amendment to the Federal and State Constitutions whereas the UNKO and USNO considered a two-thirds majority would be sufficient).

Point 17: Representation in Federal Parliament
This should take account not only of the population of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) but also of its seize and potentialities and in any case should not be less than that of Singapore.

Point 18: Name of Head of State
Yang di-Pertua Negara.

Point 19: Name of State
Sarawak or Sabah.

Point 20: Land, Forests, Local Government, etc.
The provisions in the Constitution of the Federation in respect of the powers of the National Land Council should not apply in Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah). Likewise, the National Council for Local Government should not apply in Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah).

Additional regulations and expansion of SST scope on Malaysian businesses must be frozen or restudied, especially in the manufacturing, education, and rental sectors.

Therefore, a policy of at least 50% mandatory purchase of necessities from local producers must be introduced for all ports and contractors.

In addition, certain ports have successfully used the 15-year tax exemption status to monopolise and dominate the local steel industry worth RM65 billion annually. 

Controlling 85% of the local market by foreign companies is merely exploiting the 15-year tax exemption previously granted by the government. Now only two local steel companies remain.

To protect local interests, it is necessary to introduce SST tax to create a “level playing field” between foreign competitors and local steel industries by introducing “SST 10% For Imported And Local Iron Ore, Metallurgical Coking Coal, Coke And Abolish SST On Steel Scrap”. 

In addition, the said SST tax can replace the natural resource-destructive and non-environmentally friendly processes in the local steel sector.

This not only returns money to its rightful owner but also helps the 2026 New China Year atmosphere by clearing debts and providing angpow money to their workers.

The 2% KWSP deduction for each foreign worker and employer starting October 2025 is very burdensome and must be stopped. 

The 2% income dividend tax exceeding RM100,000 must be imposed only on Bursa Malaysia-listed companies or public-listed companies, not on non-Bursa Malaysia or private companies.

7. Abolish the RM10,000 Fine Under Section 45F SIP for Foreign Worker Insurance (SIP) in State Assemblies

The amendment to Section 45F of the Workers’ Insurance Act imposing a RM10,000 fine on employers for each foreign worker without insurance is too burdensome on employers. This penalty section must be abolished when the SIP is discussed in the State Assembly.

In fact, as of 4 December 2025, PERKESO is trying to collect employer arrears with a 2-year moratorium on enforcement and proposes that the RM10,000 penalty per worker will only be imposed after the leave session is conducted with the employer and interested parties. 

A 2-year moratorium has no meaning because ultimately the RM10,000 penalty per worker will still be enforced.

Furthermore, the PERKESO statement is questionable because the responsibility all this while has been fully placed on the employer even though it has not been discussed and passed in the People’s Council. This is an act of PERKESO not conducting leave affairs with the relevant parties as required.

This raises the question why the leave session on SIP is only conducted by PERKESO after the SIP has been passed by the People’s Council and not before? 

This recommends a process of completing the SIP and must be discussed with the implementation on SMEs because the current high penalty is only reduced to RM100 per non-SME company.

8. 40% Sabah Revenue Must Be Resolved Within the Current Term and Sarawak Rights Must Continue to Be Protected

The 40% Sabah revenue claim is one of the main issues in the recent Sabah state election. This issue must be resolved and the money returned within the current term so it is not seen as merely delaying tactics by the federal government. Sarawak state rights must also continue to be protected.

9. Study Exempting SMEs from E-Invoicing and Raise the Annual Revenue Threshold to RM5 Million

The people’s demand is to exempt SMEs from the e-invoicing implementation and if it must be implemented, raise the annual revenue threshold for mandatory e-invoicing from RM5 million starting 1 January 2026.

10. Special Tax Payment Tribunal for Individuals and SMEs

Taxpayers, both individuals and SMEs, often complain that they are pressured by LHDN officers to the point of being threatened with court action by the Lembaga Hasil Dalam Negeri (LHDN). 

Such actions are unreasonable because they are unable to fight LHDN with the high costs involved.

It is proposed that LHDN increase efficiency so that the country can truly enjoy it, and it is also suggested to set up a special tax payment tribunal so that justice is done fairly with a level-playing-field status. Therefore, this Tax Payment Tribunal status should be established to ensure rule of law and justice is given to all parties.

I hope the above 10 matters will be given due attention. Thank you very much.

Point 1: Religion
While there was no objection to Islam being the national religion of Malaysia there should be no State religion in Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah), and the provisions relating to Islam in the present Constitution of Malaya should not apply to Borneo.

Point 2: Language
* a. Malay should be the national language of the Federation
* b. English should continue to be used for a period of 10 years after Malaysia Day
* c. English should be an official language of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) for all purposes, State or Federal, without limitation of time.

Point 3: Constitution
Whilst accepting that the present Constitution of the Federation of Malaya should form the basis of the Constitution of Malaysia, the Constitution of Malaysia should be a completely new document drafted and agreed in the light of a free association of states and should not be a series of amendments to a Constitution drafted and agreed by different states in totally different circumstances. A new Constitution for Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) was of course essential.

Point 4: Head of Federation
The Head of State in Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should not be eligible for election as Head of the Federation.

Point 5: Name of Federation
“Malaysia” but not “Melayu Raya”

Point 6: Immigration
Control over immigration into any part of Malaysia from outside should rest with the Central Government but entry into Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should also require the approval of the State Government. The Federal Government should not be able to veto the entry of persons into Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) for State Government purposes except on strictly security grounds. Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should have unfettered control over the movements of persons other than those in Federal Government employ from other parts of Malaysia Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah).

Point 7: Right of Secession
There should be no right to secede from the Federation

Point 8: Borneanisation
Borneanisation of the public service should proceed as quickly as possible.

Point 9: British Officers
Every effort should be made to encourage British Officers to remain in the public service until their places can be taken by suitably qualified people from Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah)

Point 10: Citizenship
The recommendation in paragraph 148(k) of the Report of the Cobbold Commission should govern the citizenship rights in the Federation of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) subject to the following amendments:
* a) sub-paragraph (i) should not contain the proviso as to five years residence
* b) in order to tie up with our law, sub-paragraph (ii)(a) should read “7 out of 10 years” instead of “8 out of 10 years”
* c) sub-paragraph (iii) should not contain any restriction tied to the citizenship of parents – a person born in Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) after Malaysia must be federal citizen.

Point 11: Tariffs and Finance
Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should retain control of its own finance, development and tariff, and should have the right to work up its own taxation and to raise loans on its own credit.

Point 12: Special position of indigenous races
In principle, the indigenous races of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should enjoy special rights analogous to those enjoyed by Malays in Malaya, but the present Malays’ formula in this regard is not necessarily applicable in Borneo(Sarawak & Sabah).

Point 13: State Government
* a) the Prime Minister should be elected by unofficial members of Legislative Council
* b) There should be a proper Ministerial system in Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah).

Point 14: Transitional period
This should be seven years and during such period legislative power must be left with the State of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) by the Constitution and not be merely delegated to the State Government by the Federal Government.

Point 15: Education
The existing educational system of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should be maintained and for this reason it should be under state control.

Point 16: Constitutional safeguards
No amendment modification or withdrawal of any special safeguard granted to Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should be made by the Central Government without the positive concurrence of the Government of the State of North Borneo

The power of amending the Constitution of the State of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) should belong exclusively to the people in the state. (Note: The United Party, The Democratic Party and the Pasok Momogun Party considered that a three-fourth majority would be required in order to effect any amendment to the Federal and State Constitutions whereas the UNKO and USNO considered a two-thirds majority would be sufficient).

Point 17: Representation in Federal Parliament
This should take account not only of the population of Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah) but also of its seize and potentialities and in any case should not be less than that of Singapore.

Point 18: Name of Head of State
Yang di-Pertua Negara.

Point 19: Name of State
Sarawak or Sabah.

Point 20: Land, Forests, Local Government, etc.
The provisions in the Constitution of the Federation in respect of the powers of the National Land Council should not apply in Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah). Likewise, the National Council for Local Government should not apply in Borneo (Sarawak & Sabah).

Memudakan Malaysia: Pilihanraya PBT / Local Council Election (LCE)

Antara masalah paling besar yang kita hadapi adalah isu penyelenggaraan.

Penyelenggaraan jalan, longkang, parit dan perancangan bandar. Semua ini adalah bawah bidang kuasa Pihak Berkuasa Tempatan.

Dulu Malaysia pernah ada LCE ni. 

Tapi kita hentikan sementara kerana Darurat yang berlaku pada tahun 1965.

Kita pernah tubuhkan Suruhanjaya Diraja untuk kaji keperluan LCE. 

Pada tahun 1968, Suruhanjaya ini telah mengeluarkan dapatan mereka yang menyokong LCE.

Tapi sampai sekarang kita tak sambung.

Sedangkan PBT punya bidang kuasa yang paling dekat dengan rakyat.

Kenapa kita perlukan LCE?

1. Mengangkat suara rakyat. 

Hari ini, rakyat bawa isu isu penyelenggaraan infrastruktur ke ADUN / MP.

Sebab utama adalah kerana mereka tidak kenal Ahli PBT. 

Mereka cuma kenal wakil rakyat yang mereka pilih.

Masalahnya tugas ini bukan bawah bidang kuasa ADUN & MP.

Sekiranya Ahli PBT tak nak bekerjasama dgn ADUN & MP, sukar untuk ADUN & MP selesaikan isu ni. 

Bila rakyat kenal Ahli PBT, mereka salur aduan terus ke Ahli PBT. Angkat suara mereka sebaiknya.

2. Fokus bidang tugas.

Kebanyakan isu yg dibawa ke pejabat saya adalah isu di bawah bidang kuasa PBT.

Maka ramai ADUN & MP tak dapat jalankan tugas hakiki untuk melihat polisi dan undang-undang.

Sepatutnya ADUN & MP perlu ada pegawai penyelidik untuk bantu gubal polisi.

Tetapi wang yang terhad perlu digunakan untuk melantik pegawai aduan yang mengendalikan aduan aduan PBT.

Sebab itu, banyak ADUN & MP hilang fokus pada tugas hakiki mereka.

3. Akauntabiliti.

PBT menerima bajet yang besar setiap tahun. Kerana bidang tugasnya yang besar.

Maka kerja-kerja perlulah dijalankan dengan baik demi kesejahteraan masyarakat setempat.

Tapi kita sering berdepan dgn isu penyelenggaraan infra yang lemah. 

Namun yang perlu menanggung beban ini adalah ADUN / MP yang sebenarnya tiada saluran langsung terhadap isu isu ini melainkan mereka adalah EXCO / Menteri. 

Bila wujudnya LCE, wujud akauntabiliti.

Rakyat boleh persoalkan terus kerja-kerja yang dibuat oleh PBT. 

Pada masa yang sama, rakyat juga lebih jelas tentang tugas ADUN & MP.

Tak wujud lagi ADUN & MP yg kata mereka sibuk dengan kerja kerja PBT  sebagai alasan tidak menjalankan tugas hakiki di Dewan. 

Semua ada akauntabiliti terhadap tugasnya sendiri. 

Saya faham bahawa ada banyak lagi kerisauan tentang Pilihanraya PBT.

Tapi sebenarnya kerisauan kerisauan ini boleh diselesaikan. 

Banyak kajian yang telah dijalankan & cadangan penambahbaikan telah diberikan.

Paling utama, budaya penyelenggaraan infra awam perlu dibaiki.

An energized country needs to have a fully functioning public infrastructure.

This calls for a healthy maintenance culture that can come from better and higher accountability.
After the rain, the sun will reappear. There is life. After the pain, the joy will still be here.

PROFESSOR AKINBILE IS NEW DEAN SCHOOL OF INFRASTRUCTURAL, MINERALS AND MANUFACTURING ENGINEERING

The Management of the Federal University of Technology, Akure, FUTA, has appointed Professor Christopher Akinbile of the Department of Agricultural Engineering as Dean, School of Infrastructural, Minerals and Manufacturing Engineering (SIMME) for a term of two years effective August 1, 2025.

The appointment is sequel to his election at the meeting of the School's Board of Studies held recently and approved by the Vice Chancellor, Professor Adenike Oladiji.

Professor  Akinbile was born in Ikire, Irewole Local Government Area of Osun State, Nigeria on 14 December 1975 to the families of late chief Abimbola Olugbenga Akinbile and madam Felicia Abosede Akinbile. He earned a Bachelor of Engineering in Agricultural Engineering from  the School of Engineering and Engineering Technology (SEET) Federal University of Technology Akure (FUTA) in 1999. Thereafter, he proceeded to the University of Ibadan where he obtained both his Masters and Doctoral degrees in Agricultural Engineering with specialization in Soil and Water Engineering in 2001 and 2009 respectively. 

Professor Akinbile joined the services of FUTA from University of Uyo as a Lecturer II in the Department of Agricultural Engineering in October, 2004 and rose through the ranks to the position of Professor in October 2016. 

He was a post-doctoral fellow at the Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM) from 2010 through 2011, a visiting scientist to Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM) in 2015 both in Malaysia and on the ticket of the World Academy of Sciences (TWAS). The same TWAS fellowship took him to Lyon, France in 2011, Ebenecity, Mauritius in 2014, Beijing and Shanghai, China in 2019 and to many other places.

 Professor Akinbile is also a recipient of the Israeli Agency for International Development Cooperation in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Mashav) to Rehovot, Israel, Volkswagen Foundation to Germany, and the Netherlands Fellowship programme (NFP/NUFFIC) to the Netherlands. He is also a multiple award winner of the Global Young Faculty (GYF) fellowship to South Africa, ICTP/TWAS to Gaborone, Botswana and to other countries such as Ethiopia, Egypt and the United Kingdom.

 He is a recipient of many awards such as the International Fellowship award to participate at the first US-Africa Frontiers of Science, Engineering and   Medicine Symposium, held in Nairobi, Kenya in 2022 and FUTA Vice-Chancellor’s Award for Remarkable Achievement for outstanding contribution to the development of the University in 2012.

Professor Akinbile has over 100 publications and one of his publications won the Wiley Awards for Top Cited Article 2020-2021 in Atmospheric Science Letters. He has also been commended by FUTA’s Vice-chancellor, Professor Temidayo Oladiji for having over 2,000 Google Scholar citations. 

He delivered the 135th Inaugural lecture series of FUTA on the 21st of September 2021 titled 'The Wealth of Waste: from Water to Rice'.

 He has two intellectual property (patents) to his credit and has won several national and international grants including the COMSTECH-TWAS Joint Research Grant, and Institution-based-research (IBR-TETFund) research grants. 

Professor Akinbile has supervised to graduation 10 doctoral, 17 Masters degree and over 90 undergraduate students. He has assessed Readers and Professors in many universities both within and outside Nigeria and also examined many Bachelor, Masters and Doctoral dissertations in many universities all around the world.

Professor Akinbile has served and still serving in different committees and positions within and outside the university. He is a member of the Tertiary Education Trust Fund TETFund’s National Research Fund (NRF) Screening and Monitoring Committee (NRFS&MC) and also Secretary of TETFund National Research Fair (TETFair), a sub-committee of the NRFS&MC that conducted the first national research fair in Abuja, Nigeria in November 2024.

 He had served as the National Universities Commission (NUC) appointed member of accreditation panels to some universities in Nigeria and also served as a volunteer mentor to the Federal Government’s Youth Enterprise with Innovation in Nigeria (YouWin) program (2010-2012) under the dispensation of Dr. Goodluck Ebele Jonathan GCFR, the then President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.

Within FUTA, he is the Chairman of FUTA Sports Council, Member, University Publications Committee, Appointments and Promotions Committee (A&PC) and former Associate Director of the defunct Centre for Entrepreneurship and Gender Issues in Science and Technology (CEGIST). Similarly, he was the Chairman of Abiola undergraduate male hostel, served in the joint Council-Senate Selection committee in 2022 and many other committees. Within the School, he had served as Chairman of Sports committee, TETFund committee, Postgraduate coordinator and others.

Internationally, Professor Akinbile had represented the country as an international facilitator to the Institute of Security Studies of the African Centre for Peace and Security Training (ISS-ACPST) based in Ethiopia, invited lead speaker to the 17th CAS-TWAS-WMO Forum on Climate Science (CTWF), International Symposium and workshop on Ecohydrology and Climate Change, hosted by the International  Centre for Climate and Environment Science (ICCES), Institute of Atmospheric Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), Beijing, China. He also served as young scientists’ coordinator to the Communication event for the climate change adaptation and resilience in Africa policymakers held in Ebene Cybercity, Mauritius and many others.

Professionally, Professor Akinbile belong to many associations such as, Fellow of the Nigerian Society of Engineers (NSE), Fellow of the Nigerian Institution of Agricultural Engineers (NIAE), Fellow of the Nigerian Science Leadership Programme (N-SLP), Fellow of the African Technology and Policy Network (ATPS) and Fellow of the African Academics Network (AAN).

He is a registered professional engineer with the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN) and also a member of the American Society of Agricultural and Biological Engineers (ASABE). Professor Akinbile is a member and Editor-in-Chief of Pan African Society for Agricultural Engineering (PASAE) newsletter, national executive council (NEC) member, national technical secretary and Editor-in-Chief of NIAE newsletter. 

His hobbies are reading and watching soccer. 
Professor Akinbile is an ordained minister of the gospel and is married with children.

Professor Christopher Oluwakunmi Akinbile is the first elected Dean of SIMME and also the first alumnus to be so elected into the position.

SPECIAL EDITION - MALAYSIA DAY 2024 

TIMING OF MALAYSIA 

By William Goode
Jesselton, North Borneo, 7th April, 1962

1.It can hardly be disputed that North Borneo is not ready for Malaysia. The Proposal came as a shock to people who were occupied with developing their own country and had no wish for change. It must take several years at least to develop political leaders, to introduce elections, and to produce a local civil service. In North Borneo’s interest, a transition period of several years is needed before Malaysia is put into effect.

2. This will give time to prepare North Borneo for the change and will enable Malaysia to be built on firmer foundations. Are there any objections to the delay as far as North Borneo is concerned?

3. The first objection raised is that delay will allow the Communists to gain strength. Hitherto the communists have failed to establish any organisation in North Borneo. This is because there have been no emotional issues for them to exploit and no organisations to penetrate: no burning desire for freedom; no anti-colonial movement; no class struggle; no issue over Chinese schools; no trade unions; and until very recently no political parties. As political parties develop, they will provide opportunities for Communist, penetration but at present, the danger is small. Malaysia itself provides the best cover for Communist penetration since there are strong popular feelings against, Malaysia and it has aroused racial fears which can be exploited. The Communists will certainly exploit Malaysia, but, they will profit more from a Malaysia rushed upon an ill-prepared North Borneo, than from a transition period of careful preparation.

4. A second objection is that delay will allow opposition to Malaysia to gather strength. This objection assumes that further consideration of Malaysia will increase opposition rather than persuade those who are now reluctant or suspicious. On the contrary, more time should make it possible to secure a better understanding of the true worth of Malaysia and to overcome present doubts and fears by explaining how North Borneo's interests will be safeguarded. Delay will also remove the accusation that the people of North Borneo were rushed into Malaysia without, being given time to understand its full implications.

5. Another objection is that North Borneo's political leaders will develop a vested interest against surrendering power to the Federal Government. This can be prevented by not allowing any vested interest against, Malaysia, to grow up during the preparatory period. The principle and the broad outline of Malaysia should be agreed now, and the gradual transfer of authority from the British Government and officials to local leaders can then be made in accordance with the agreed final division of authority between the State and Federal Governments. During the preparatory period, North Borneo leaders should not, be given any powers they will not retain when Malaysia is introduced.

6. As far as North Borneo is concerned, the advantages of delay greatly outweigh the disadvantages. Would delay cause insuperable difficulties outside North Borneo?

7. The immediate urgency over Malaysia arose from the political situation in Singapore. Nine months ago Mr. Lee Kuan Yew's Government appeared to be disintegrating; it, was feared that he would lose his majority in the Assembly and be forced to a general election, which would result, In the Communist dominated Barisan Socialis gaining power. Only merger with Malaya and firm control by the Alliance Government, could prevent, the Communists capturing Singapore and then getting full independence from the British Government. But for internal political reasons, the Alliance Government could not carry out merger of Singapore without, at the same time bringing the Borneo territories into Malaysia. Therefore, Malaysia must be introduced rapidly because only immediate intervention by the Alliance Government will prevent the Communists capturing Singapore.

8. Today the situation in Singapore has improved. Mr. Lee Kuan Yew has beaten off the Barisan Socialis attack and exposed their Communist direction. There is no immediate likelihood that he will be defeated in the Assembly. There is no apparent, reason to prevent his Government running its full five year course to May 1964. The Barisan Socialis have lost a series of battles with the P.A.P. Government: Chinese school examinations, the City Council strike, the Workers  Brigade , and in the Assembly. Their strength comes from success and without success it is likely to wane. They have had no success since July last year. They have no capable Members in the Assembly and no obvious way to maintain their momentum. Their present, tactics of repeated pin prick strikes are likely gradually to alienate public opinion. Nor has the Singapore Government, yet, used the sharp weapon of arrest, of the known Communist, leaders and organisers, though Mr. Lee Kuan Yew stated recently that, the time was approaching when this weapon could be used without damage to the Government' s political strength. The removal of its Communist organisers would wreck the Barisan Socialis. This weapon is available now too the Internal Security Council. But, it should be used at the most favourable time. The Communist, leaders should, if possible first, be stripped of popular support. This Mr. Lee Kuan Yew seems to be doing. If he can win a referendum on merger and Malaysia is accepted by the British and Malayan governments and the majority of the people of the Borneo territories, then Singapore will probably accept merger as inevitable and abandon the lost, cause of opposing it. The Communists will be left on their own.

9. Ironically the only immediate danger to the P.A.P. Government now apparent arises from merger: the referendum. Presumably the longer this can be delayed, the better is the prospect that the Barisan Socialis Influence will be eroded and the referendum won. Alternatively, if Mr. Lee Kuan Yew judges that he can win the referendum, he can hold it. If he wins, then he has beaten the Barisan Socialis and secured his position. If he loses, presumably merger cannot be forced upon Singapore and the whole project of Malaysia will have to be postponed,

10.Singapore remains a problem and a threat, to Malaya. But there is no immediate crisis. indeed, it could be argued that, the better plan is give Mr. Lee Kuan Yew longer to beat the Communists politically and to take Singapore into merger with the support, of public opinion rather then risk losing a referendum this year; nor should the Tunku, if he can avoid it, take repressive action against the Singapore Communists while they are able exploit, the merger issue and appear as the champions of the interests of Singapore against subjugation to a Malay government in Kuala Lumpur.

11.On this assessment, a postponement of merger for a year or two in the interests of the Borneo territories would not weaken Mr. Lee Kuan Yew' s position. It would also give him an excuse to postpone his referendum, if he so wished.

12.How far does the Singapore general election affect the timing of Malaysia? It has been assumed that Malaysia and merger of Singapore and Malaya must be achieved before the general election in Singapore due in 1964. Presumably the arguments underlying this assumption are that, after merger the Singapore electorate will vote more sensibly and reject the Barisan Socialis end the Communist, and the Alliance Government, will be able to arrest Communist organisers if this is needed before the elections.

13. The first test will come in the referendum which must be held before merger. It must also be held before Malaysia is put into effect, since the Tunku has said that if the referendum rejects merger, he will not, go on with Malaysia. Therefore, Malaysia is only possible after a successful referendum in Singapore.

14. But if Singapore accepts merger in a referendum, the Barisan Socialis and the Communists will have been defeated. It would surely then be unlikely that the Communist,s would capture Singapore in the election. Mr Lee Kuan Yew will have won a decisive victory and be in a much stronger position to counter the Communist threat. Moreover with merger accepted by Singapore , and Malaysia accepted by all concerned for introduction after a short preparatory period, the Singapore Government and the Internal Security Council would be better placed to arrest and detain Communist leaders if necessary.

15.Lastly, it is hard to see how merger could be successfully carried out by a Singapore Government, facing a general election and possibility of defeat on the issue of merger. The sounder course for the future of Malaysia would surely be that Singapore should first confirm its acceptance of merger in a general election and elect a Government with the political strength to carry it out.

16. Alternatively, if the Tunku considers any delay in Singapore to be too dangerous , it is open to him go ahead with the merger of Singapore and Malaya as soon as Malaysia has been agreed in principle and the main features of the constitution settled, without, waiting for Malaysia to be fully carried out in North Borneo.

17.There is also the problem of Brunei. At present Azahari has successfully mobilised public opinion against Malaysia. It is uncertain whether or not the Sultan will be prepared to commit Brunei to Malaysia against the wishes of his people; or whether he could maintain his position if he did. He is committed to elections this year. The result, could be decisive. The Sultan is probably waiting to see what happens in Sarawak and North Borneo. If as a result of the Cobbold Commission both these territories accept Malaysia, the Sultan may then feel that he can take Brunei in too; if the other two do not accept Malaysia he can postpone the issue in Brunei . If Malaysia is accepted in principle for Sarawak and North Borneo and the main terms agreed now but a period of several years granted in which to effect the change, Brunei will still have to reach its own decision, There is no reason to think that delay in carrying out Malaysia would prejudice that decision.

18. It is at least arguable that, delay in carrying out Malaysia would not prejudice the situation in Singapore or in Brunei. On the other hand, if Malaysia is rushed, fails to work satisfactorily, and is rapidly discredited, its failure must, have serious consequences in all the territories concerned.

Extract: A Letter dated 7.4.1962 to Cameron Fromanteel Cobbold, 1st Baron Cobbold KG GCVO PC DL was a British banker. Local Council Elections are a Rakyat's Priority!

Personally, I have a neutral view about Local Government Election in Malaysia. Race shouldn't be an issue considering most local governments are Malay-Muslim dominated except for in large urban areas such as Petaling Jaya, Pulau Pinang, Johor Bharu, Ipoh, Kuching, and Kota Kinabalu among others. 

But before we support local government elections, we need to ask ourselves, what powers do local governments have? What are local governments? Local governments in Malaysia consist of:
1. Dewan Bandaraya (City Hall) or Majlis Bandaraya (City Council)
2. Municipal Council (Majlis Perbandaran)
3. District Council (Majlis Daerah)

If a local government election is to be held, all of these local governments will be involved and most of them are Malay-majority areas.These are areas where PAS will likely dominate hence PAS can implement their usual policies on alcohol, gambling outlets, and entertainment. 

In fact, this may provide a passage for PAS to penetrate into Muslim-majority areas of Sabah, and Johor. So perhaps, PAS should consider mellowing their stand on local government elections.

On a side note, many supporters of local government elections argue that local governments will be made transparent to provide good service with great efficiency. 

However, there's a major fallacy to this argument. Many cities in Europe such as Paris, Berlin, Brussels, and London have issues related to rent, waste management, gentrification, etc. despite local government elections. This can also be seen in places like New York City, Chicago, Seoul, Jakarta, Manila, Vancouver, Los Angeles, and a few other places. Hence, local governments will not guarantee good service and security.

I am in no way implying that local government elections don't work at all. Zurich, Stockholm, are some examples of places where the local government does work.

Another point to discuss is the jurisdiction of the local governments. Although Malaysia is a federation, most powers are concentrated in the hands of the federal government such as education, public transportation, healthcare, police, and taxation. In the case whereby state power is already limited, local governments have even more limited power.

In places like Switzerland and Sweden, most of the income taxes go to the local governments. In some other cities and local governments, they are able to collect sales tax as well.

These are just some concerns and thoughts I have about local government elections.

Even Nik Nazmi himself admitted that the MPs of Kuala Lumpur may be majority opposition. This suggests that the election could easily become a tool for a political party to insert loyal politicians into power structures. When politicians control who can run, the election becomes a competition among elites, not a mandate from the rakyat. 

PSM is firmly opposed to this as this bill:
- Restricts community participation
- Risks political dominance by whichever party holds majority of MPs
- Makes election symbolic, with real decision-making still in hands of politicians
- Continues the practice of a political KL Mayor, not chosen by residents
- Does not guarantee inclusivity, transparency, or representation of civil society

This will essentially reinforce the status quo of political influence within DBKL and work against the intention of reviving genuine local representation in governance. 

PSM stands true to its stand that local council governance should give back power to the rakyat: 
- To choose leaders who  understand and champion community needs, not corporate or elite interests.
- To promote inclusivity , highlighting that politics is not only for the elites, but the working class too. 
- To enhance transparency in urban planning, budgeting, and development approvals to empower the rakyat and decentralised political power.

This aligns with the original practice of local democracy prior to 1970 in Malaysia. PSM calls for the government to return power to the people, so that local governance becomes a vehicle for social justice, equitable development, and true democratic representation.

Yazid, Treasurer of Pemuda Sosialis

KOTA KINABALU: A citizen-driven, nonpartisan initiative which seeks to empower Sabahans to voice their concerns, propose solutions, and play an active role in shaping policies will be held from March to June.

The three-month-long initiative called "Sabah Voices to Action – Shaping Sabah’s Future Together" will be officially launched by Sabah Action Body Advocating Rights (SABAR) on March 19. SABAR will facilitate inclusive sessions and compile recommendations to be presented to political parties ahead of the 2025 Sabah State Election.

“This will be done through multi-platform engagement, including podcasts, newspaper publications, regional town hall meetings, and a culminating conference.

In addition, six Regional Town Hall Meetings will be held from April to May in Kota Kinabalu, Sandakan, Tawau, Kota Marudu, and Keningau, offering Sabahans a direct platform to voice their concerns and ideas.

The initiative will culminate in a Final Town Hall Conference in June, where stakeholders will consolidate recommendations into the Memorandum of Sabah Priorities.

“The ultimate objective of this project is to promote an inclusive, transparent, and participatory policy-making culture in Sabah by fostering a bottom-up approach to governance,” said SABAR Board Chairman Datuk Zainie Abdul Aucasa.

He said it aims to shift the political culture by encouraging transparent, rational, and professional policy discussions that engage experts, stakeholders, and the public in co-creating solutions to Sabah’s challenges.

Organising Chairman Lim Hock Song said through open dialogue and collaborative decision-making, the initiative seeks to cultivate a proactive, professional, and inclusive nation-building culture, ensuring that policies reflect informed discourse and the genuine needs of the people.

He urged Sabahans to stay updated on the latest podcast episodes and town hall event schedules by following SABAR’s Facebook page and visiting SABAR’s official website.

“Join the conversation and be part of shaping Sabah’s future through inclusive and participatory policymaking,” he said.

The initiative is supported by Daily Express as the official media partner, ensuring widespread coverage and public engagement.

Daily Express Chief Editor Datuk James Sarda welcomed the collaboration, emphasizing the importance of media fostering meaningful discussions on public policy.

“Daily Express has always been committed to providing a platform for informed discourse on Sabah’s most pressing issues,” he said.

“This initiative aligns with our mission to promote awareness, civic engagement, and accountability in governance.

By amplifying expert insights and public voices, we hope to encourage constructive dialogue that leads to real, impactful change for the people of Sabah,” he said.

Meanwhile, the initiative will be officially launched on March 19 with the release of the first episode of an 8-Episode “Sabah Voices to Action” Podcast Series, hosted by Kopitiam Council and SABAR.

Kopitiam Council is a podcast hosted by Sabahans Mohd Hafizul and Aidil Putera, exploring global and local affairs and their impact on Malaysians, especially Sabahans. Through bold discussions, they break down complex issues—from politics to social trends—offering fresh insights into the forces shaping our world.

Following each podcast episode, Daily Express will publish special newspaper columns featuring extended discussions and expert insights on those subjects.

Their collective expertise will provide crucial insights into the healthcare challenges in Sabah, contributing to informed discussions and actionable solutions.

Mayoral and City Council Election May 2023

Alhamdulillah hari ini berpeluang mengundi di Mayoral dan City Council Election bagi memilih councillor dan Mayor. Saya mengundi bagi councillor ward Humberstone and Hamilton dan Mayor bagi Leicester. Kalau di Malaysia ni macam Dato Bandar dan Ahli Majlis lah. Cuma di Malaysia bagi kedua jawatan ini akan dipilih oleh kerajaan negeri. 

Pilihanraya ini disertai oleh banyak parti dan wakil bebas. Antara yang sertai adalah Labour Party, Local Conservatives, Liberal Democrats, Green Party, Trade Union Socialist Coalition, Conservative Party dan Independent. Kertas undi memang panjang berjela lah. 

Proses untuk sertai pilihanraya ni mudah. Mula-mula pihak local council akan ingatkan kita untuk daftar mengundi. Buat online sahaja. Then confirmation pendaftaran akan dihantar secara pos. Bila dah dekat tarikh mengundi, poll card akan dipos kepada kita. Kita akan dimaklumkan kat mana kita nak mengundi. Cara mengundi pula boleh undi hadir, undi pos atau undi proksi. Maknanya orang lain yang kita wakilkan boleh undi bagi pihak kita. Tapi kita kena maklum awal kalau nak undi selain dari undi hadir. Kami memilih untuk undi hadir. Waktu mengundi agak panjang dari 7am - 10pm. Fleksible bagi memudahkan semua orang untuk mengundi. 

Mayoral Election ni tak meriah mana. Brochure calon dihantar terus kerumah. Takde banner, poster dan bendera parti. Kemudian kalau nasib kita baik, masa kita nak pergi mengundi adalah calon yang akan tunggu kat pusat mengundi. Masa saya nak mengundi, ada 2 calon councillor yang ada kat lokasi. Amik peluanglah jugaa bergambar dengan mereka. Local mosque ada beri cadangan siapa nak diundi. Calon yang lebih mesra kepada semua agama termasuk islam. Supaya mudah aktiviti Masjid nak dilaksanakan. Alhamdulillah pengalaman menarik dibumi Inggeris.
